utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. If you could call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, General Miletic is not present today. We have a waiver already. The other accused are present. Prosecution today, we have Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Vanderpuye, Ms. Soljan. Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Nikolic in the Beara Defence team; Mr. Bourgon in the Nikolic Defence team; Mr. Lazarevic in the Borovcanin Defence team, and that's it. Any preliminaries? No. Mr. McCloskey, the Borovcanin Defence team has filed, as promised, the motion relating to a particular document. Do you think you are in a position to respond orally today?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, good morning. Mr. Thayer had that in his hands last night, and we discussed it briefly. If I can check with Mr. Thayer about that, I can get back to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If it is not possible for a response today, perhaps you could discuss, also, with Mr. Thayer the earliest you could come back to us with a response. Thank you. I'm talking of P4104. All right. Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Marojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I should have addressed you as Professor Marojevic. My apologies. Before you start giving evidence, we require from you a solemn declaration that you will be speaking the truth. Please read out the text that is being shown to you now, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Haynes who is lead counsel for General Pandurevic will be putting some questions to you, and then he will be followed by others on cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor Marojevic, and good morning to everyone else. You know who I am because we met yesterday. I'm counsel for General Pandurevic. Can we start, please, by establishing what your full name is?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Radmilo Marojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And for the first time, you're going to have to look at the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that we put 7D778 into e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can you look through that, please, and confirm that that is an accurate summary of your professional life and experience?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: The birth place is not Markovac but Morokovo. And the same goes for primary education; Morokovo, not Markovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But after that, can you look at what you've been doing principally since 1973?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: And after that, philological faculty and the faculty of political science and MA degree, all right, and PhD degree, all right. Now, in the work experience, right. The information is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And how do you currently spend your time?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm a professor at the Belgrade university, and I lecture also at universities in Banja Luka and Nis. My specialty is Slavistics and especially the textology of verse and other literary works of Petar Petrovic Njegos, a great Serb poet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you know or have you ever met Vinko Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In this case, we know from a report you've written that you came to analyse two documents that have concerned us. How did you come to be involved in that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drago Cupic telephoned me and asked me to receive Mr. Djordje Sarapa in connection with a textological analysis of a document, and since this is my primary area of expertise, I accepted Mr. Sarapa, and that was around new year 2006, explained the matter to me. And since I accepted in principle to do it, sometime later in February 2006 I received a text of the combat report dated 15 July, and I looked for another text that may have been written in the same genre signed by the same person. And later, that must have been in the summer of 2006, I received another report of the 16 July, so that I thought over these text and as it usually happens in such cases, each element of the texts required a lot of thinking, and I started writing in September 2006. And sometime in the beginning of 2008, my work was complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In addition to the two documents you've spoken about, did you meet Mr. Sarapa on occasion?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Very seldom because Mr. Sarapa did not visit Belgrade often at the time when I was there because I spend around five months a year in Montenegro. Plus there was no particular need for us to meet because the text itself was quite sufficient for analysis. The only thing I never received and I never even expected to receive is a different interpretation of that text. I could only suppose which parts of the text could give rise to some different interpretations than those which were authentic. Of course, I knew what it was all about. In fact, I knew how the Tribunal was established and in what languages it worked, so I could suppose that the text would not be interpreted only by native Serbian speakers, which means Serbs of Orthodox, Catholic, or Islamic faith, which use the language regardless of various renamings of the language; but it would be interpreted also by people who speak English or other languages. And it is well known that foreigners who have a superficial knowledge of Serbian or read texts only in translation can sometimes have a different understanding. That is why I looked at it -- I looked at the text from that perspective and tried to imagine what other broader interpretations are possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you require and get any information from Mr. Sarapa about the texts?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: A scholar who wants to identify a text would act in a methodologically proper manner only if he disregards completely any outside suggestions. Of course, I had to ask Mr. Sarapa about the provenance of the texts; namely, I had to ask him to explain to me the abbreviations and acronyms at the beginning of the text. Perhaps I could have found out in some other way, but that was not necessary. Namely, ZV stood for Zvornik, but I could make out myself that BR is brigade, et cetera. I did not need anything else and Mr. Sarapa did not volunteer anything else. He only asked me to provide an authentic interpretation of the text, and I was well aware that scientific truth like any other truth is the best contribution for the Tribunal to enable them to make the right decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And is that an exercise that you had performed in the past?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I performed similar analyses, some of them published. For instance, on an authentic critical interpretation of any dark, unclear spot in The Mountain Wreath by Njegos, I also interpreted a famous Serbian ballad The Mournful Letters of Hasanaginica, and I did the same thing for the Russian epic of The Igor Regiment as well as other Russian epics and Slavic texts. I also made interpretations of Slavonic texts, and none of these interpretations have ever been disputed. In my work I use, of course, all past interpretations of the texts and I quote past interpretations so that all the arguments could be exposed to comparison. And whenever I quote an argument, I also cite whether it has been proven or not, and if it's a controversial argument, I point out where the controversy lies. Now, this text is relatively easy to interpret because it is written in a clear and concise way. It belongs to the official legal genre of combat reports, and there was practically nothing in it that would give rise to differing interpretations. Everything is clear and unambiguous based on the methods normally used to authenticate texts, primarily the text in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just to clear up a couple of things with you. Do you speak English at all?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: At the philological faculty of our university, I sat two English exam, English 1 and English 2. I got top marks on both exams, but I had no opportunity to use the English language because in my field there was practically nothing to read in English. However, since it is not so necessary in my field, I have no emotional link to the language; therefore, I would appreciate if you would address me in Serbian, in Russian, or some other such language.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm not even going to try. And in what language did you write your original report?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: In Serbian. And I did not check, although I could actually check the translation into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And similarly, what knowledge do you have of the events in and around Zvornik of the 15th and 16th of July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did not know anything about the specific events, and the first I heard of the surname Pandurevic -- in fact, no. Some of my students in Banja Luka have the surname of Pandurevic, but the first I heard of Lieutenant-Colonel, later General Pandurevic was when I was asked to write this report. I know very little about the events concerned, only as much as one can know based on available published material. What I know very well and what is not the subject of this analysis is the new world order. I know very well the scenario developed in Srebrenica. I know very well that the envoy of the new world order Clinton asked Izetbegovic that everything be done to create a trap for Serbs and entrap them into genocide. I know very well and I explained that in my book "The Cyrillic Script At the Crossroads of Centuries" in 1999. I maintain that, and that has scientifically proven that in Bosnia-Herzegovina there is only one people living there, and the new world order made up a nation called Bosniaks. There is only one single nation or people there who speak a group of very similar dialects, all of them being Serbian. So in Bosnia-Herzegovina there are Serbs of Orthodox faith, Serbs of Islamic faith, and Serbs of Catholic faith. However, to prove a genocide it was necessary to invent a pseudo-nation; first of all, Muslims with a capital M, and later, Bosniaks, although Bosniaks has no meaning at all. Bosniaks are in fact Bosnians, an archaic prototype. I knew all that, and I anticipated all that in my study of 1991 when I spoke about who the Serbs were, which names are used to denominate Serbs, et cetera. And the details of the implementation of that scenario around Srebrenica were totally unknown to me because in that period I spent most of my time in Russia. I visited, of course, and lectured in Pale and in Banja Luka occasionally, but I was not so interested in the details. I knew that this scenario of the new world order was being implemented in Srebrenica, not only by Serbs of Islamic faith and foreign mercenaries, but there must have been, also, Serbs of the Orthodox faith involved, so I could not suppose either of these things. I had to see what this text means, whether there are any hidden meanings or not. Unfortunately, I see that in this Tribunal of ours, if it is ours at all, there is no Mr. Clinton. You see, when somebody is responsible for an entrapment into genocide, then we don't have the person responsible. We don't see the Dutch Battalion here. The only accused are some of the possible perpetrators or some of those who fell into the trap of that scenario. Therefore, in Srebrenica and in the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina, the war was ignited from outside and the objectives are completely different. The objective is to accuse the Serb people of genocide, although there could have been no genocide because there is no other people. All of them are Serbs: On one side, Orthodox Serbs; on another side, Serbs of Islamic faith; and on the third side, Serbs of Catholic faith. Of course, in the earlier times, there had been Serbs of the Moses faith, but they have joined the Serbs of the Orthodox faith in the death camp of Jasenovac. Wiesenthal has said enough about -- Wiesenthal does not even mention them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have 7D917 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can you identify that this is the linguistic analysis you wrote of the reports of 15th and 16th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm this because I have a version which is part of your material and another one that I downloaded from my computer, and they are identical. Of course, what I consider authentic is only the text in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you explain to us what it was you understood your task to be in preparing this report?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: I understood that my task was to carry out a linguistic analysis of the text, i.e., to carry out the textology of the combat reports, which means that all those places that might be in dispute or are interesting from the point of view of a linguistic analysis should be explained by me. In any case, the objective of the analysis has been presented in the paper. The objective is to show the basic meaning of the passages where prisoners of war are mentioned. I believe that it was of some significance for the analysis of the text and also to put that passage in context of other passages speaking of the situation on the ground and the basic tasks of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. My third task was to present the textual and contextual relationship between the interim combat report of the command of the Zvornik Brigade dated 15 July 1995 at 1925 and the interim combat report of the command of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade dated 16 July 1995 at 1810 hours. So these were the frameworks within which I was to carry out my analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I want to go directly to the report of the 16th of July. I'm not going to take you all the way through your report, but just to clarify a few remarks in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So can we go to page 12 in the English, please. That's section 8. I think the page is the same in the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell me what B/C/S is? What is B/C/S? Please could you use Serbian instead of B/C/S, and I don't care whether that Serbian is going to be the Ijekavian or Ekavian variation, and to show you that I really don't care, I used my Ijekavian variant in my report, but in the courtroom I will use the Ijekavian because that's how people speak in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This will facilitate my analysis. An exception were the combat reports because in the Yugoslavia's People's Army it was customary for the text to be written in the Latinic script but to be spoken in the Ekavian variant of the language.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, you've probably answered my next question, which is that in relation to the report of the 16th of July, you have said at the foot of the report that it was written in one dialect but typed as the appendix to your report in another, and I was going to ask you to explain that. If there's anything that you've left out, would you do so now?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to say that this report was written in Ekavian because -- what I meant is that the linguistic analysis was written in Ekavian because the report which was analysed was also written in Ekavian. It was written in the Cyrillic script, and that's why the linguistic analysis was also in the Cyrillic, although it is not obligatory, but it is, of course, desirable. The second text which is brought in connection with the first one by intertextual analysis was written in Ekavian with certain elements of Ijekavian. I established, which was not at all difficult, that this was under the typist who probably was Ijekavian and who obviously had not served in the army for any longer time because if he had served in the Yugoslav People's Army, he would have had to be well versed in writing, typing, and speaking Ekavian because that was the language of command in the JNA. Obviously, I took into account the fact that such errors may have been made by somebody who was Ijekavian but not the person who dictated the text. In addition to that, the errors and mistakes are completely understandable because where there is a two-syllable reflex of "jat" involved, there are no mistakes there. For example, look at the words "cele", "linija fronta". In the Ekavian, it would be "cijele." The difference is between "cela" and "cijele." The mistakes appear where the differences are not in the number of syllables, so for example when somebody dictates an interim combat report, an Ijekavian will use the word "isvijesta" [phoen] with a J as it has been done here. So there is a combination of Serbian literally language, but this did not have a bearing on the commander or did not originate from the commander but, rather, from the incorrect spelling on the part of the typist in the second text, whereas the typist of the first text noted the text exactly as it had been dictated to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how much difference does it make, the two dialects?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: These are not dialects at all. These are two literary expressions. The first one was established by Vuk Stefanovic Karadzic, and at first it was the only literary pronunciation or expression of the new literary Serbian language. And then in the 19th century, some 20 years or 25 years after Vuk's death, the Ekavian literary expression or pronunciation was introduced, but it was identical with the Ijekavian, the only difference between that the reflection of "jat" were replaced with the Ekavian expression, which means that the fundaments of both of these speeches were taken from the Niksic of the eastern Herzegovina, i.e., from the boundary between Montenegro, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Serbia. The Ekavian is not based on the Ekavian dialects or speeches but, rather, on the Ijekavian speeches. This is one and the same literary pronunciation with two variations. In spontaneous speech, these two variations are so minutely differentiated, and if you don't pay much attention you will not even know whether the person is speaking Ijekavian or Ekavian. These two are so close that they constitute one in the same Serbian literary pronunciation or language.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just two other observations --

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we go to section 5 of the report, which is page 5 in the English, and I think 6 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You've said a little about this already, Professor Marojevic, but you've characterized the interim combat report of the 15th of July as an official legal text, and I'd like to you to help us as to what the characteristics of such a text are.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, an official legal functional style is one of the five functional styles which exists -- which exist in the Serbian and other Slav languages. What are the other functional styles? There is a scientific functional style which is used in science papers. Then there is conversational functional style. Further on, journalistic or publicistic style, and of course the literary or artistic functional style in writing. And like all the other styles, this particular style, the official legal style has the strictest structure, which means that it does not tolerate elements which are typical of a jargon or a conversational language. This is a style in which one needs to formulate one's thoughts very clearly. It is a style in which you do not omit anything that shouldn't be omitted according to the linguistic rules. And finally, this is such a functional style in which one strives for a complete lack of ambiguity, which means that it has the same -- the same meaning for the person who writes the text as well as for the person who is going to read it, and in our case, for those who will be interpreting it or use it to charge a person or defend a person charged with certain acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: If you stay with that paragraph for a little while, you go on to talk about each paragraph in the report being a semantically meaningful unit. Would you expand upon that just a little bit, please?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of this paragraph number V entitled the "Structure of the Interim Combat Report 15 July 1995," which was the subject of my linguistic analysis, when it says in this paragraph that every paragraph represents a meaningful whole, it says further on that this meaningful whole is composed of one, two, or several sentences. If every paragraph were to represent or constitute or consist of just one sentence, then meaningful wholes would not exist because every sentence would be a paragraph. This is one criterion that helps us to establish that one paragraph is one whole and that the text is very regularly divided into passages. The second criterion is as follows: Where there are two or several sentences, these two or several sentences could be divided by full stops or commas, and they could be condensated into complex sentences. And a third criterion that could be proven here very easily is this: There is no way for the text to be connected from one passage to another unless the whole text was completely changed. In other words, all the arguments presented here point to the fact that the paragraphs are independent wholes and that whoever dictated the text and whoever typed it did not make a single mistake of connecting two paragraphs into one or breaking one meaningful paragraph in an artificial way into two different wholes. In other words, all the paragraphs function as a totally independent logical and semantic wholes. They could also be syntactic wholes if the genre itself did not warrant for the text to be as precise and possible. What makes a text precise is to put full stops everywhere where a semantic units ends, and this provides for a completely transparent and clear meaning of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You have alluded to it in your answer, but were you aware of the process by which the two documents you looked at were created, namely by dictation?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: In this sense, it may be concluded that the text was dictated and that whoever typed it did so based on the dictation. It can be assumed that the person who dictated the text and, as it is customary in the Serbian pedagogical discourse, also spelled out the word full stop where the sentence ended and that preceded every new paragraph with the words "new paragraph." The second possibility that exists, and that would result in a text of this kind, was that the person who dictated the text had already prepared a draft, a concept, a structure of the report and that he knew exactly where the paragraphs would be because he had already prepared an outline, and that made it easier for that person who dictated the text to draft this text which functions as a whole and looking at its part, it represents a very well structured composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we go to page 7 of the report in the English, please, which I think is page 8 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In chapter VI of your report, "Linguistic Analysis Of the Text," you pose yourself four questions. I'm not going to read them out. I'm sure you're familiar with them. Why did you pose yourself those four questions in that chapter?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I think we need to go back one page in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph entitled "Linguistic Analysis of the Text," which is the central part of this linguistic analysis, I posed those questions which I deemed to be of some interest for the understanding of the meaning of this text. The first question is this: "This command cannot take care of these problems any longer..." This has been singled out as a particular paragraph. I had to show in contextual terms what are the problems referred to within this text in order to avoid any confusion or misinterpretation especially if the reader's language is not Serbian. I wanted to show that this refers to the previous paragraph, and I provided arguments to show that this does not refer to the previous or, rather, not the immediately preceding paragraph but, rather, to the first five key paragraphs. The sixth paragraph was just a remark in passing, and if this had been a different genre of a text, if this hadn't been an official legal document, and if this hadn't been an interim combat report, then the preceding paragraph could be construed as a footnote. It could have been taken out from the text and included at the end of the text because it is just an additional burden on the text. This had to be said. This had to be explained. My next question was whether -- or, rather, what is the function of the word "security" and the "asnacija" of the terrain. If the punctuation is correct, and we don't have any reason to doubt that, security could not stand on its own if it was not separated by a linguistic mark. We had to explain what is the nature of that security. Was it something that was independent, and what was its meaning, or was it this providing security for the terrain, meaning "asnacija"? And then we had to explain the link between "release" and the rest of the text, and whether the word "release" can have the meaning of setting free from the prison. I had to explain the context in which "release" can be used in one or the other meaning because there are words which have their own independent meaning when they are used independently and have a different meaning which can be used only in a colocation. There is this word "release" or "let go," so you can use it as, Did you let them go, and to let go or release from the prison in a conversational language can be construed as release of prison only if the word "prison" is used. In an official document, this does not mean to be released from prison. You cannot let go from prison in a legal text without using the word "prison." One can only free prisoners. He cannot just let them go. And given the possibilities that the Serbian language inambiguously demonstrates, and I have used the best six volume dictionary, the Serbo-Croatian dictionary, as the Serbian language was known at the time; the authors of that dictionary worked on a huge database, and they could not know at the time, they could not even assume that somebody would try to give the verb "release" or "let go" a meaning that would be misinterpreted here in this Tribunal. The lexicographers had provided the structure of the word "release" a long time ago, and if this confirms what the linguistic practice showed to them, which can be verified by experiments without any exceptions, then one really needed to explain the relationship with the word "release" or "let go" with the next paragraph in which it says "let everybody go through," or -- and whether this "let go" can have any connection with the prisoners which were referred to in the immediately preceding paragraph or footnote as I have just called it, and the analysis of course will show very clearly without any dilemma whatsoever, and what I'm using for the analysis of the meaning of this verb and I'm using not one but all sorts of methods in order to establish its meaning, although only one method suffice. However, I used all the four methods because the four methods absolutely clearly show that the analysis is correct. If this was not about the Tribunal, if this was not about an expert report, if this was merely a linguistic analysis, then it would suffice for me to say or use just one sentence in a footnote. "Let go" cannot mean "liberate" unless it is further expanded by saying, Let go somebody who had been captured. There is an anecdote about a person who had captured an enemy, and then he calls his friend and says, I captured him; and the answer is, If you had captured him, bring him over. And then the first one says, He doesn't want to go. The second says, If he doesn't want to go, then let him go. And then the first says, I would let him go but he doesn't want to let me go, which means if you capture somebody, you tie his hands or restrain him in another way. You can then let him go. But you cannot use the verb "let go" in reference to a prisoner. There's no indicator to show that this verb can have this meaning. There is no single example for that. Obviously, I have taken into account only the things that may be of relevance for the Tribunal. There is a dictionary of the Croatian or Serbian language, but it is a historical dictionary. I didn't want to have this taken against me. I did not quote from the historical dictionary, but it would prove exactly what I'm saying. It is impossible. There is not a single example to show that verb "let go" can be used with this meaning. I have also used a large database of the dictionaries of the Serbian and Croatian literary and languages of the Serbian academy of arts and sciences; however, that dictionary did not reach the letter P, which would stand for the Serbian "let go." However, everything in the database, and there are a lot of examples, that illustrate my claim that the verb "let go" cannot independently stand for "release" or "set free" from prison on the one hand; and on the other hand, in any case it can mean let somebody go out, in, or through. So that this analysis was obviously indispensable for the text to gain its full meaning, not only for a linguistic expert and not only for the native speaker of the Serbian but for all the others, as well, for those who learn the Serbian language, for those who interpret into English, and for those who use the English text in order to understand the Serbian language and charge the Serbian language with what it is not and what it shouldn't be blamed for. There is no word "let go," which would also mean release from imprisonment. So it is in vain to accuse the Serbian language of that attempt, and I'm here to defend the Serbian language in a scientific manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have a look, please, at page 16 of your report in English, 18 in Serbian. Maybe 17 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This is paragraph 3 we are looking at, Professor Marojevic, of the interim combat report of the 16th of July, and I want to look with you, please, at the penultimate sentence, which reads in English: "I requested that a captured policeman and my missing soldiers be released." What verb is used by the author in that sentence?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, first, a clarification: It's not the penultimate; it's the third from the end. It's not for me. It's for the opposite side; maybe they will say that it's not in the penultimate sentence. We have to be clear for the sake of the structure of the text itself. The word used is "oslobodjenje," to be released. It's a verb noun. It's a gerund. In Serbian, you could say, I asked that the captured policeman be released. But instead it was said, I asked for the release of the captured policeman. It's perfectly clear. The verb is "osloboditi"; the verb noun is "oslobodjenje." It is used in the proper style, and, of course, it is not replaced by the "let go" verb, "pustiti," "pustanje"; the proper word is used. That is the proper word to be used to denote that meaning. "Osloboditi," "oslobodjenje," meaning release from imprisonment. In the old language, it was not "sloboda" for freedom; it was "svobode," but that's the only difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What significance do you ascribe to the fact that the same author used that same in this context in this report but "pustiti" not once but twice in the report of the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: That's just the sign that in the previous report the word was not used in that meaning. That meaning was not present, and since there was no such meaning, the word corresponding to that meaning was not used. What was said there was that everybody should be let through, let pass, let all of them go because we see from the prior passages that the commander was willing to let all the civilians go, and then later let everybody go, including those who were armed. Let all of them get out. That's why I asked for this post-dated text, which sheds light on the previous text from the semantic and from the lexical point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to move on to a couple of other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have a look, please, at 7D109.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And it's a fairly straightforward question. You talk at length in your report about the conceptual link between the word "oslobodjenje" and the word "terena" in one of the paragraphs of the combat report. In this document, the second and third words of the text we see are "oslobodjenje teritorija." Is there any difference in meaning between the words "terena" and "teritorija" in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, these are synonyms. Practically in every context you can use to secure territory and to secure terrain as mutually interchangeable words. Territory and terrain are not 100 per cent synonyms. They are not always used in exactly the same meaning, but to secure territory and to secure terrain are complete synonyms. These colocations are absolute synonyms. The only thing I could say here as a textologist is that in this right-hand text, it's written "for the purposes of securing territory" because what it says in the original is "teritorij" instead of "teritorija," and "teritorij" is the Zagreb variant, and the proper Zagreb genitive would be "teritorija." In any case, securing territory and securing terrain is one in the same meaning, and they are always interchangeable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Staying with that for a minute, can you help us as to the etymological derivation of the word "obezbedjenje"?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: "Obezbedjenje," or in the Ekavian variant "besbijadjenje" [phoen], is a Serbian word, but it was taken over originally from the Russian word "abispecinja," [phoen] and the Russian politicians often put the accent in the wrong place and say "abispecinja." It can be used in all sorts of meanings. It can mean securing terrain from landslides; when rain starts and rock and soil give way, the terrain needs to be secured. But in this meaning, it's always a transitive word. You cannot say secure; you have to say, Secure what? It is a feature of the Serbian language but not the Russian language, which is the source, that "obezbedjenje" has another use which is independent, not transitive. In our days we have the security service, and by abbreviating the colocation we can just say security or meeting service. However, the origin of "obezbedjenje" is the Russian word "bezopasnost", and Security Council in Russian would be "Sovjet Bezopasnosti," and our language developed in many ways under the influence of the Serbian literary language but also the Czech language. Both of these are Slavic languages, one of them eastern Slavic, another Western Slavic, and they impacted both the variant used in Zagreb and the basic variants, Ekavian and Ijekavian used in Belgrade, Podgorica, and other Serbian lands. So the conclusion here would be that "obezbedjenje teritorija": Is the same thing as "obezbedjenje terena," securing the terrain. But with regard to "asnacija," in combination with security, the rule is strict and the whole sentence would read "to secure and clear up terrain": "Obezbedjenje I Asanacija Teritorija." I can interpret this text by saying that "obezbedjenje teritorija," securing the territory, is one meaning; and if I had another text, I could have used it to establish intertextual connections because intertextual connections cannot -- are not necessarily between two texts made by the same persons, but two texts in the same language.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one final thing on that issue. You said earlier that "obezbedjenje" is always a transitive word. "You cannot say secure; you have to say, Secure what?" What do you mean by a transitive word?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, a transitive verb is defined as a verb used with an addition in the accusatory case, but there are verbs that can be used without that addition or with. They are also transitive verbs. However, purely transitive verbs cannot exist without that addition. What is the difference? The difference is very important. To read and to read a book: "To read" is a transitive verb. It may and does not have to have an object. If I say I'm reading a book, then "to read" is one part of the sentence and the book is the object. "To secure the territory" are not two elements of the sentence; it's one because "I secure" means nothing unless I add "territory." In this case, syntactic analysis shows clearly that I'm securing territory or securing terrain. All of this is the subject of the sentence. If the linguistic analysis cannot separate the two, the law cannot do it either. If you separate these two words, then the meaning is lost. It's not only a transitive verb. It's a transitive verb that requires an object, a noun in the accusatory case so that it's called a paraphrastic element. This is not idiosyncratic; it exists also in English, but it's not the English language that's in the dock here. It's not only the Serbian people who are in the dock, but the Serbian language is accused, as well, of having to carry the meanings that somebody wants to impose on it. I guarantee that it has no such meanings. I have defended the Serbian language before, and I successfully defended it from attempts to expel the Ijekavian variant from the Serbian language in Bosnia-Herzegovina whereby it was attempted to prove that Serbs were the aggressors there, and I also successfully defended the Ijekavian dialect as an integral part of the Serbian language. I successfully defended Njegos from fallacious interpretations, and I hope that ultimately I'll be able to defend the Serbian language here from erroneous analysis. Securing terrain is one syntagm, securing territory and securing terrain. Everything is clear and logical here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think I'm done, but can we take a break so that I can check that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's a good idea, Mr. Haynes. 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I have no questions for this witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. I do have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Marojevic. My name is John Ostojic, and I represent Ljubisa Beara in this case. I have a couple of questions for you. And sir, at the outset, although I'd like you to know that we do not agree on the many things that you have said, especially the political rhetoric and the philosophy that you've shared with us today, but I'll try to move away from that and focus on your report. Sir, with respect to the experience that you have, can you tell us how many cases you have testified in in court as an expert?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: I've never been in this Tribunal before. This is my first time, and this is the first linguistic analysis I've ever performed for this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What about outside this Tribunal, any other courts anywhere in Belgrade or former Yugoslavia or Russia or any other place you may have lectured or studied?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. I've never appeared before any other court, and I have never provided any linguistic expert analysis for any other courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. How about the topic of the linguistic report that you conducted here, and I understand from your proofing note that was conducted yesterday, you state that you analysed many things, something other than poetry and literature. Now, I'm familiar or I've looked up some of the analysis you've done with respect to poetry and literature, but have you ever analysed an official text, as you call it, official fundamental style as one of the five fundamental styles that you discuss in your direct? Have you ever done that before, or is this your first time as well?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course I've analysed Russian Pravda Dusan's Code of Law, the letters that were sent to poet Njegos by the ruler of Montenegro. There were no limitations in genre, but official legal texts are not of such an importance for the history or culture such as literary texts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So you have really no experience whatsoever in analysing official legal texts, correct, with the exception of this case here that you've given us, this report; and really, your emphasis or concentration, if you will, is strictly in the poetry and literature arts; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Nothing of what you have just put to me is true. I have performed analysis of the constitution, the law on associated labour, and these analyses are part of my bibliography. Second of all, there's no other linguist, and I am aware of that, has ever performed such analysis. I have been the only one to do them. For somebody to carry out such analysis, that person has to have some knowledge in philology but also in the subject topic of the area to which such an official legal document belongs. If you have studied my bibliography, then you must have seen that I graduated from the school of political sciences, and at that school one has to study all the relevant legal subjects, and I completed those studies together with the study of philology at the same time, which means I have all the necessary qualifications to perform a linguistic analysis of legal texts, and I've done that. Legal text in legal terms because of the genre that I've already explained are not such to mandate scientific discussions. You can also read my very first papers that were published in the students' paper in Belgrade where I analysed the constitution and its amendments from the linguistic point of view. None of those analyses were ever challenged. Your question, however, is not good, is not properly formulated. What you are trying to say, actually, is if something didn't do something in the area but in an associated area, an area which is 28.000 times harder than a legal text. If one is to analyse a literary text, they have to be aware of the essence of the literary text. For somebody to analyse a legal text, they have to be familiar with law. When I studied political sciences, I passed all the exams within the legal area with the highest degrees, and I would like to add, if I may, and I think I may, your first question and my first answer to that question was whether any other linguist has every analysed any text of this type. The answer is no. Why not? Because a linguist has also to be an expert in economy and law to the extent of being able to understand the essence of the text. I've done that, although this was not exactly the narrow scope of my interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's narrow it further, then. How many cases have you been retained or that you've analysed that focus specifically on an official military combat report such as the one that you've done here? How many other instances? If you can be brief, that may help me out with the time constraints that I have. Many? None?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can't lead me in answering your questions. I defended two doctoral theses about a scientific functional style, which also comprised texts that are of interest to you and to all of us here, and those dissertations were about the syntax of a scientific style in the Russian and Serbian style by candidate Andrej Stojanovic and the stylistics of the verb by Professor Tosovic at the University of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, and I'm sorry to the panel of Judges and Mr. President. I just want to know how many times you've analysed an official military combat report other than this one time? Just give me a number, whatever it is. How many, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Your question has no deeper meaning because nobody has ever analysed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'll move on because I think we know the answer to that question. Let me talk about your political affiliation, sir. Presently, are you affiliated with any political party?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: At one point I was a member of the Serbian Radical Party when I was appointed as the dean of the school of philology. At that time, Mr. Seselj expressed his wish for me to become a member of the Serbian Radical Party, but this was just a formality. I never participated in the work of the party. I participated in three scientific symposia to defend Mr. Seselj. The symposia were held in Belgrade. I also published two articles in the paper The Greater Serbia, and I also published several studies mostly about Njegos in the magazine, The Serb Freedom Thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll get to your appointment as dean in 1998 and 1999 at the University of Belgrade while you were with Vojislav Seselj's party, but presently are you a member of any political party? And you can answer yes or no, or you don't know, maybe.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I suppose if I were a member of the party, I would be able to answer you, sir. I never withdrew from the Serbian Radical Party; however, if they don't invite me to their meetings or don't offer me any jobs to do, I would say that I'm not an active member of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, you said you analysed some constitutional laws and all this. In May of 1998, are you familiar with a law that was passed in Belgrade immediately prior to you being appointed dean of the faculty of philology in Belgrade called the University Law? Are you familiar with that act or enactment?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: That was not its name, but it was about that area, that's the law that came into effect. I studied it immediately as a philologist, as a politologist as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Here is what many people have said in the press about that specific act. They said that: "It's seriously undermines academic freedom and the autonomy of Serbian universities." I can get you the exhibit. We have about five of them that discuss you in particular as being the extreme linguist who adopted and promoted that type of philosophy. Do you agree with that, that that University Act that was enacted in May of 1998 actually undermines academic freedom?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: I totally disagree. This law did not undermine academic or any other freedoms. It only prescribed that all university professors and other members of staff had to sign a work contract, and that work contract was an incentive for those who worked for the others. And it is well known that opposition parties were all on the payroll of foreign intelligence services at the time. On the other hand, you mixed some things. You say that I'm an extreme linguist and so on and so forth. My linguistic activity has nothing whatsoever to do with the work I performed as the dean of the school of philology. This is not correct. May it be seen that the new administration that was instituted in Belgrade in 2000 have retained the same law and university, and that law was in effect for a long time, and those new parties came as a result of Puc. And these new authorities, the new administration which were instituted in Serbia -- I apologise, I'm not finished. The new authorities, when they were evaluating the law in university, they stated that the only person who fully implemented the law was Dean Radmilo Marojevic. I was at the time duty-bound to implement the law of my state, and my maxim was "dura lex, sed lex," and that means that even a law may be bad, one has to implement it. I was also trying very hard to pin-point its weaknesses and if possible amend them. In addition to that, those who were duty-bound to sign the contract under the law, I said I would be the one who would not sign it. You have to because you are duty-bound. If I don't sign it, your obligations will not come into effect. Your information is wrong, and if it is correct, then you have to tell me how were the academic freedoms threatened? The Belgrade university and other Serbian universities had such a legal procedure imposing the signing of the work contract. What was restricted by the work contract? No freedoms or liberties were restricted by the work contract. All the other states and I'm sure you belong to one and that your state and its universities have similar laws that prescribe that a member of the faculty has to sign a contract on rights and obligations when joining that faculty.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I don't want to spend too much time on that, but you're familiar with who Professor Ranko Bugarski is, are you not? Because when you talk about contracts, that's one name that should come right up to shed some light for you, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Ranko Bugarski is a sociolinguist in Belgrade. He graduated in English at the moment when I was appointed the dean of the school of philology. He met all the criteria to be retired, and the previous dean had extended his work contract by two years, and when I became dean, I issued a decision that this contract would be valid until the 30th September 1998. And after that, Ranko Bugarski while I was dean no longer lectured at the school of philosophy in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But he was fired, sir, despite of the fact immediately prior to May of 1998 he had a two-year extended contract, and you fired him in essence because of his opposition to the nationalistic policies or politics that were prevalent in Serbia and Belgrade at that time; isn't that accurate?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, none of what you have just said is true. I can give you evidence that there were others who criticized then government of Serbia and its policies, and I never fired them. It was just about the implementation of the law on universities. Since Mr. Ranko Bugarski was a sociolinguist who did not meet any criteria to call himself that, for somebody to be a sociolinguist they have to be familiar with the methods of both linguistics that he is not familiar with and sociology, which he also isn't familiar with. And as for the work of Ranko Bugarski, if you are not informed about that, I criticized him already in 1991 in a book of mine. His work was just the rephrasing of some fashionable works from the western literature and had no significance whatsoever for his teaching of English language. As the dean of the school of philology, it was my duty to protect science and profession, and I know at the extension of his contract, I had realised that he should no longer be allowed to institute harm to science and the professionalism at the school of philology.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's just quickly look at 2D649, please, and it's in English, but I could read the paragraph that relates to Professor Bugarski for you unless you would like to read it for yourself. It's going to come up on your screen, and it comes up on the second page on the top of this. This is a publication, sir, that I found from the AAAS Science and Human Rights Programme, which discusses in September of 1998 this academic freedom and the new law that was enacted in Belgrade at that time, upon which you became the dean of the faculty. And as it's coming up, I think I can just begin by reading from my text if no one objects. It says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It says on the top here, it says: "The appointment of Radmilo Marojevic as the new dean of the faculty of philology, also a member of the SRS ..." which is the Serbian Radical Party, "... and the junior professor of Russian, Mr. Marojevic determined that a prominent linguists Professor, Ranko Bugarski, who is a critic of nationalistic policies, was no longer eligible to work at the university, even though he had signed a new two-year contract in May 1998. Although Professor Bugarski has the support of other faculty member, under the new law, Marojevic has the authority to nullify his contract. While the consequences of Marojevic's efforts are not yet clear, such arbitrary actions have a significantly negative impact on the academic climate." Are you familiar that's what people were writing about you, sir, when you became dean of the faculty in 1998?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, at the time a lot more was written about Dean Marojevic than about Milosevic and Seselj together, which means that the new world order and its servants were bothered by the scientific and constructive position that I advocated at the time. And as far as Professor Bugarski is concerned, there had been changes in all postgraduate studies in Serbia, Montenegro, and in Republika Srpska, and the curriculum of post-graduate studies were derobed of the totally unnecessary subject, general linguistics, that is part of graduate studies. So the services of Bugarski were no longer needed. For scientific reasons, therefore, Ranko Bugarski had to have his contract modified - not nullified, but modified - and was made to be valid until the 30th September, 1998. It was completely legitimate. Mr. Bugarski never filed an appeal against that decision, and there was no other possibility to contest a decision or challenge the decision which was based on a profession, science, and moral, and the decision that was made by myself as dean.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you another publication, which is 2D647, which is from a source called Times Higher Education, which is THE, is the acronym. And on that one, again, 2D647, it says the following, and I'll wait a minute just so it can come up on the screen for you, and that's the middle of the paragraph. It talks about your conflict that you had with the students' federation and with another student organisation called Otpor. You recall those organisations, do you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course I remember. The leader of that organisation Otpor was a former student of the school of Germanistics who has never graduated until this very day. And that former student or maybe even current student participated in the occupation of Serbian television on the 5th of October. This organisation Otpor was a militant fascist organisation who was in charge of demolishing everything and preparing the occupation of Serbia. In addition to that, you are talking about students, and let me try and convince you or the Trial Chamber by saying that of those students, only a dozen of them remained, and finally, I negotiated with those students to see what their problems were. And their problems were the fact that they did not like some of the provisions of the law. And then I told them, Okay, we have to implement the law that is in effect, but we have every right to ask for the amendments to the law. And all of those students -- and I swear to you once again that this is the truth, and everything that I have said so far has been the truth. In Serbia, if you give your word, your word is your bond. This is a part of the concept of the Serbian culture, let me just tell you in passing. All the students agreed with that meeting to end that students' strike, to ask for the amendments to the law. I enjoyed a lot of respect in the government at that time, and I could do that. However, unfortunately, those students must have had some other ties, and overnight they had been consulted by their partners and, you know, sir, that the international organisations bribe our politicians and our students, as well, and unfortunately those young people who had promised to me that they would talk to me and everybody else, finally they didn't. And just for your information, all these students when they come across me in the street, they speak to me with reverence, and also, the professors had obligation, and in order -- instead of quoting what you have, I refer to Allen Dulles from 1945 who says that is every possible means would be used to destroy the Soviet union; in this case, the supplies to the Serb countries. Please find the doctrine of Allen Dulles who subsequently was the director of CIA, and according to his doctrine, the Soviet union would be destroyed together with all the other free countries, and he tells exactly how this would be done. One of the things would be to bribe all those who are prone to bribe. Those who could be blackmailed should be blackmailed, and if anybody remains who understands their plans - I didn't say yours, I said theirs; I hope they are not yours as well - then we would proclaim them insane. As the dean of the school of philology, I was the first one to introduce into a Serbian university the so-called Serbistics as a science of Serbian language and culture which had not existed before or since. For your information, there are Russian studies, there are Slovak studies, English studies everywhere. That's what the names of those subjects are. The only that cannot exist in Serbia is the science of Serbian language, culture, and science. That's the only thing that is not to allowed to exist in Serbia at Serbian universities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ostojic, and my apologies to you for interrupting you. Professor Marojevic, you are being asked very simple questions, which in our mind could be answered very simply, too, in a couple of sentences. As it is, you are giving very lengthy answers which are not helping anyone. So I would suggest that you keep your answers as short as possible, and try not to deviate from the substance of the questions that are being put to you by Mr. Ostojic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, we were talking briefly about the student federation and the organisation Otpor, and you mentioned the student's name. Do you remember his name? I think the first name was Branko. It's in the Article that I pulled, which is in front of you, 2D647. Do you remember his last name?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You mentioned someone in your response to my question just moments ago, although it was quite lengthy, where you said there's a student there who was organising it, and he didn't even get his degree, and then even to this day he probably didn't get his degree, but you weren't that sure. What student were you talking about? You must know who it is since you know he didn't get his degree.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: I know, but I forgot his name and surname, but I saw him after the 5th of October participating in the occupation of one Serbian TV station. In addition, he --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. We don't need all that information, but thank you, and I apologise for cutting you off. Let's look at this exhibit 2D647, which is the Times Higher Education where they mention you among others who are the new deans that were appointed to universities at Belgrade. It says here in the middle part of it, and it talks about this young student Branko having joined an organisation wanting to express some of his freedoms as a student and -- both political and academic freedoms that he was looking at, and it says about you here: "Initially he ..." meaning Branko, "... joined the students' federation, which was independent of the state, but the dean of philology faculty Radmilo Marojevic, a member of the extreme Serbian Radical Party of former para-military leader Vojislav Seselj, tried to shut the Federation." Then it goes on to say that this young student joined another organisation, Otpor. Did you, sir, ever try to shut down that student organisation?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: God forbid. I didn't try to shut it down. On the contrary, I supported it. It was the students union that first proposed me as a student vice-dean back in my student days.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It talks -- sorry about overlapping. It talks in this article about a protest, in essence, that was held with approximately 80 students and that 15 thugs were hired, they claimed by you, sir, to beat up those students in order to prevent them from protesting or expressing their free speech or any academic rights that they have may have. It says here, if you read down, that the organisation Otpor blamed the dean for the violence, meaning you, but Professor Marojevic denied he was responsible for hiring the thugs. It guess on to say: According to the Belgrade newspaper Blic, Professor Marojevic said their orders, meaning of the thugs, had come "from the top." And then it goes on to say: Nevertheless, he was forced, meaning you, to quit his job under a hail of press and public criticism. And now I want to ask you two questions about that, if I may. First of all, sir, when they use -- or quote you from the top, who made the order -- and I will.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One by one, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please let him the question first. When you interrupt, you are creating a lot of problems for the interpreters that have to interpret what he is saying into your language and into French. Plus, it is not allowed here to interrupt anyone. So Mr. Ostojic, my apologies to you. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, and I'm sorry. I did overlap, and I'll try not to, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: They're quoting you -- Blic is quoting you, although it's published in the Times Higher Education publication, as saying that the orders to beat up these students who were holding demonstrations or protests, and they quote you, sir, by saying that the orders came from the top. I'd like to know exactly from whom do you know that those orders came from to beat up these young men and young women, actually. Three were injured -- women, three women were seriously injured in that altercation. Who gave that order?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Just after this clash occurred between two groups of students, I submitted my resignation to the post of dean of the philological faculty. Who organised that group of students that tried to force another group of students out of the hallway, outside of teaching hours, I cannot tell. I can only suppose it was ordered by the CIA. Nobody in the authorities knew about it, and I myself was not aware that any of the students are being moved by force, let alone beaten up. It was not our style, never has been. Even before that, there had been many student protests. These protests were rather innocuous. They were almost over, and just a small group of students remained that didn't create any disorder. They just didn't want to leave the premises, and then somebody put in another group of students, and a clash occurred. And since I was completely unable to find out who was responsible for that, and now I can only suppose that it was the CIA, which also organised various political parties, since I was unable to find out, I had to resign because I could see that I couldn't do anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, I wanted to change topics, if I may, with you briefly. I want to talk about the contacts that you've had with the Pandurevic Defence team. You've told us that there were few or several of them. Can you be more precise for me? Can you tell me exactly how many times you met with the Pandurevic Defence team, whether their lawyers or investigators or assistants, in total?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, investigators, assistants, I never met, and I never met Mr. Pandurevic himself. If I could make a request of the court, I would request that General Pandurevic get to his feet so that I can meet him for the first time. I only had contact with attorney Djordje Sarapa, and the first contact was at the suggestion of Dr. Drago Cupic, former director of the institute of the Serbian Academy of Art and Science after the new year, or translated from Serbian into Serbian; it was either before the new year or after the new year according to the Julian or the Gregorian calendar, sometime around new year 2006. And soon afterwards I first saw the text that I was supposed to analyse. And the next time was in the summer when I received the second text. So the total of encounters with attorney Djordje Sarapa were several, and to translate it again from Serbian into Serbian, it is not several, which would mean seven or eight or more. I said it in a form that would mean three, four, or five, not more than five.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Who was present at those three to four meetings with Mr. Sarapa, other than yourself and Mr. Sarapa, obviously?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Nobody was present, just Sarapa and Radmilo Marojevic. No one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How long did these meetings last, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, these encounters were very brief because I didn't have much time. Everything was pretty clear to me, so these meetings took 10 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that the combat report of the 15th of July, 1995, is clear and concise; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: I can say that it's concise, as well, but I used actually another word, which means easy to grasp.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I can go with that, too, easy to grasp. Well, if it's clear and easy to grasp or even concise, why would we need someone to interpret something that's plain and obvious to us? I mean, typically - don't you agree with me, Professor - it's the ambiguous sentences or words or thoughts that we would need assistance on, but if something is clear as you say this July 15th, 1995, interim combat report is, why would we or the Court or anyone, for that matter, including the lawyers of Mr. Pandurevic need someone to explain it?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: No, sir. Absolutely any and every text that is explained in a scholarly way in an attempt to give a textological interpretation requires a textology. There is no text that doesn't have a textology. So this text, too, is very interesting for a textological analysis, and when an analysis is done, how would I know whether a text is clear and lucid as opposed to textologically ambiguous if I hadn't done an analysis? Please don't think that I first wrote that it was clear and lucid and then performed my analysis. The fact that I wrote something in the introduction does not mean that I came with it as a preconceived idea. It is the result of my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you've told us in your report and in some of your testimony that you've done this textual analysis using four different supposed methodologies; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say different. I said all the four methods that can be applied in establishing the authentic meaning. All these four methods were applied in this text analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's go through some of them in better detail so I can get a fair appreciation. One of them is what you call lexicographic description, and that's basically even as you define it as looking up words in the dictionary and observing and perhaps even digesting their common meaning. Would that be fair? That's one of the methods that you used?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: The method of lexicographic description is not exactly as you put it. If a lexicographic analysis is correct, it is an indicator of a general meaning of every lexic unit. In addition, to analyse a text that was created after that lexicographic source, the analysis can also show whether the new text is completely in conformity with the analysis made on prior texts, and this is quoted here as the fourth argument, which means that before that, all the other standards had to be met to see if the fourth one conforms and whether it's correct. If the three other methods gave the same result, that means that the fourth is also correct, which doesn't mean that in some other dictionaries, for some other lexic units, especially older ones, then they not be some erroneous interpretations, but this particular interpretation is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We are going to go through each of the four. I just thought I'd start with lexicographic because I want to ask you a follow-up question regarding the separate units and the opinion that you claim that each paragraph is a separate unit. My specific question to you with respect to that, sir, is what's the basis of your opinion that each paragraph in the 15th July, 1995, interim combat report is a separate unit?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: I arrived at that conclusion based on three arguments. First of all, one paragraph does not consist of just one sentence, so that the formal syntactic whole is not the whole of the paragraph. And whenever we have two or three sentences in a paragraph in another style, such as the scholarly style, they can be combined into one complex sentence. And a third argument is, you cannot combine into one single sentence any of the segments of the previous paragraph with any segment of the following paragraph. That leads us to the conclusion that according to a semantic procedure, these elements of content are correctly divided into paragraphs. When we perform a much more complex analysis of another text, we would be able to establish by the same method whether this is a verse, a rhyme, or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to get into the poetry with you, sir, but I want to know specifically, when you used this lexicographic analysis that you did, what really goes into it if it's not simply the process of physically finding a dictionary and looking up the words to see if you have the proper definition or meaning of them? What else is involved in this analysis or methodology that you utilised, the fourth one that we're looking at, this lexicographic analysis. What else other than simply looking up the word in the dictionary?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not just looking up words in the dictionary. First of all, you have to identify the optimal dictionary or dictionaries that could be taken as an indicator of the word's value. Second, in linguistics, a lexicographic analysis is an integral part. This analysis is required from me because we are not dealing with linguists. The analysis refers to the whole article. Page 298, 299, the complete analysis is quoted, including all the phraseologyisms, which include the said verb, and it shows us how it, combination with other words, the verb takes on different meanings. And what is also analysed is the return form of the verb, such as let oneself go. Since we are not dealing with that, I didn't analyse it, and I showed that it is used here, "let go," in the second meaning, meaning be, to allow someone to do or go where they want.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marojevic, really, all I'm looking for now, if you could be as brief as possible, how long did it take you to do this lexicographic description or analysis as your fourth methodology for your report? Just give me a time estimate. Was it more or less than 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: To provide an analysis of a lexicographic source such as this one, that doesn't mean at all that other dictionaries were not checked. Some checks were not necessary, but I did them nevertheless out of academic curiosity. I checked the etymology of the word in very different dictionaries. It is an old Slavonic word, and then you use the old meanings, the examples that illustrate that meaning, and you provide a scholarly implicit critique of the scientific article. That means whether the shades of meaning are set out correctly just as the meanings themselves. For every example, you state whether that shade of meaning has anything to do with the example from the text, and only then you find the right place of your own example in that dictionary. That is where it would it be if it were used in the dictionary. However, I didn't measure that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the other three textual analyses that you've performed. The first one which you call textual analyses, you also mention these linguistics units, and we talked about who determines these units, and I want to know from you whether this was arbitrary and selective, who made a determination of these units, or was that something that is just done from a linguistical expertise, that you would say, for example, and what I'm getting at, Mr. Marojevic, is in the 15th July, 1995, combat report, you talk about how specifically paragraph 6 doesn't relate to either the foregoing paragraphs or the subsequent paragraphs of that report. Who makes that arbitrary decision, you as a linguist, or did the lawyers for Mr. Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the decision to identify a certain meaning in a text is not taken by vote or any such procedure. It is taken on the basis of scientific authority. Scientific authority in this case shows which methods may be used in the first place to identify a meaning. Therefore, somebody could attempt to question that only if they were a qualified linguist. This is a matter of linguistic analysis, which meaning it is. If it were not so, then all this would be pointless. Linguists are supposed to identify a meaning, and the lawyers can then go on to establish the relationship of that text with whatever is the subject of their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And the second methodology that you are using, which you call contextual analysis for reaching your opinions, all you're doing is looking at the one text and trying to take certain words and putting them in context with what was written within that document, like we know of 15 July, 1995; correct? That's basically the process in a nutshell?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Here we actually have two methods. I didn't understand whether you were talking about the first or the second one. Have you finished with the first one --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: -- and moved on to the second, or are you still on the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's a good point, but I'll clarify it for you. I am still on the first one. I'll preface my question when I move on to the intercontextual analysis, which is your second methodology that you used, but sticking with contextual analysis as a methodology, and I've just in a nutshell tried to summarise it for the sake of being brief here. All you're doing is taking certain words or paragraphs, and within that document you're comparing them in the whole context of what that writer is trying to convey; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't do the best job, but you are trying to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: The point is if this verb "to let" were outside of any context, then we couldn't establish anything else without etymology.
