To identify any meaning of any word, unless it's a very simple one-meaning word, we need a context. For all multi-meaning words, we need a context to establish what the meaning is in a particular case. And since I dealt, also, with the theory of translation, and in translation you obviously need to establish in which meaning the word is used, quite independently of this particular analysis dealing with translation as a method of semanticising a foreign text, I used context again. Words can sometimes be used without it being clear which of the two or three meanings they are used in. In this particular case, the context is quite sufficient to understand which of the meanings the word is used in. It is not something that is used here only. It is the first and foremost method for identifying a meaning. If a word has multiple meanings, never has it been possible to establish the particular meaning without context. If it is a simple one-meaning word, nobody bothers to analyse because the meaning is clear without any analysis. Are you happy with the answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it's not a question of whether I'm happy, sir. I just want to make sure you give us a complete answer. Let me ask you about one word in that report: "liquidation." Did anybody ask you to analyse that word, standing alone in the first paragraph where they talk about liquidating the enemy forces? Did you do any analysis on that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: I did not analyse it because the word is quite clear. First of all, nobody asked me. As I said at the beginning - and don't you think that I gave that oath lightly - when I said I analysed this text independently, I really did it independently as a linguist, but also a linguist who understands the gist of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But keeping in mind --

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Because I'm not only a linguist. With liquidation, do you want me to give you an oral interpretation of that word, or is it clear to you? Well, if it's clear to you and it's clear to me, there is no need to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have two follow-up questions staying with this first methodology, contextual analysis. Who chose the words for you to analyse in this interim combat report of 15 July?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: The words were chosen by Radmilo Marojevic, which means myself. How did I make this selection? I took the text; then I applied the method of elimination. First, I started with a broad list of the words to be analysed; and then when I eliminated straightforward words which were not in dispute even in translated into a different language, then I came up with a structure of the words which would be of some significance in scientific and professional term, which commanded explanation. And I believe that I've done my job very successfully because even you are not adding any other word to the list of those that I've analysed, and you are not saying that the words that I've analysed are clear without any further analysis, which I understand as your praise for my job well done. We didn't even have to explain the word "liquidation" because it's clear to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You may be misunderstanding me, sir, but I'm not going to get into it. I'm talking about just your methodology first; then I'd like to go into your analysis. The second method that you purportedly use in your analysis was the intertextual analysis, and what you did basically and in essence was you took one report, the 15th of July interim combat report, with the report of July 16th, 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would you agree with me, sir, that that's a rather limited way of doing things, if you're going to do an intertextual analysis that you should analyse more than one document? For example, you could have looked at reports prior to July 15th, 1995, reports that bear his name. You could have looked at the report from July 18th, 1995, as well, in order to be more complete, thorough, and comprehensive. Do you agree with that as well?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: I can't agree with you at all for the following reason: I have just said that in order to analyse the meaning of a word, you don't just need context. You need the context to be sufficient, and sufficient context can be the context of just one sentence, one paragraph, or a whole. On the other hand, when it comes to an intertextual analysis, depending on the complexity of the text, and you agreed with me when I mentioned that, when I said that this text is very articulate and clear and straightforward, you have to take a sufficient intertextual corpus in order to understand the meaning of the text. In view of what is written in a text since nothing that happened before was in dispute, the only thing that may be in dispute is what follows because this interim report, there's nothing in dispute when it talks about things past but, rather, about things that will happen in the future. In few of the intertextual analysis, I needed the subsequent combat report. I received it, and it was enough. I did not ask for anything else. Whether or not there were other combat reports was not of any consequence for the scientific analysis. You're trying to interrupt me, although I have not finished. I did not have to expanded the number of text. I did not go to go further or prior to this text. This was quite enough. The text that I analysed was enough. And no other author contested my findings, which means that the body of the analysed text was enough, the context was sufficient, and that's the end of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: All right. And I didn't mean to interrupt you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, I'm leaving it in your good judgement, of which we are very aware, to distinguish the wheat from the chaff and concentrate on what is essential, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because otherwise, we are not going to finish this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I realise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, are you still sticking to your hour and a half, or is it considerably less now?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. It will be considerably less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll move on to the next topic, and I won't debate it with you. Sir, I just want to cover this non-linguistic situation, which is the third of four methodologies that you utilise in your analysis. Just so that I'm clear, who provided that information to you, the non-linguistic situation?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the non-linguistic situation, this non-linguistic situation in some linguistic works appears under the term and concept of context. I have separated from the context that concerns the words in the text from the non-linguistic situation or information that the text points to. When it comes to a non-linguistic situation, it is not a special knowledge that one has. It is just the knowledge about the linguistic reality that the text itself initiates. You have the date, so it can't be the 19th century or the 11th century; then the name, the Zvornik Brigade is given, so this could not have happened in Siberia or elsewhere. This is what the text initiates, and then the genre, combat report. You can't talk about psalms or some other text because the text itself points to the non-linguistic situation rather than anything else. So this is not something that I could know as the author of the linguistic analysis. This is a non-linguistic situation that every native speaker or foreigner who understands Serbian will completely understand based on the text and the insight into the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's focus specifically, although I don't know that I got an answer, but on P329, which is the 15 July 1995 interim combat report, so I'd just like to direct your attention. You spent a lot of time, obviously, reviewing it and analysing it. The sentence we're going to look at it the one that you analysed. It says: "An additional burden for us is the large number of prisoners placed in schools in the brigade zone as well as obligations of security and sanitation of the terrain." Now, in your report it says sanitation. In the actual P329, the document that was translated, it says "restoration." So forgive me if there's a little difference there, but I think we can clarify that. I don't think it's that major for our purposes and our discussions. I want to look at -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hold it. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I can interrupt. That translation has been the official CLSS translation for many, many years through many cases. It's very important, and so I wish we can keep that the way it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I don't object to that. I just don't want to necessarily engage in a discussion as to which is proper. I'm going to stick with P329 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think I should say that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him finish. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This report was translated by the Tribunal as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That wasn't the purpose of me asking him that. I just wanted to point it out to the court in case anyone has a question or concern about it, and I don't want to -- if he's used it a different way, that's his analysis, and we can go through it. I want to focus on other parts of the document, but we're sticking with P329 as the official one if that's what my learned friend suggested it is. We don't have a dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just don't want to get the witness more confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, try to simplify matters because the situation may get out of hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, in this sentence that we're referencing here, the noun, do you recognise the word "prisoners" as being a noun?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: The question is so self-explanatory, and I don't need to answer that. Of course it's a noun. Why should I confirm that? If I did, somebody may say later, Well, there was Professor Marojevic claiming that "prisoners" is a noun. I can give you the origin of the noun. It's a non-substantive -- that would be a question for me, not whether "prisoners" is a noun. Of course it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry. Sometimes we just don't want to take too many chances with witnesses. Now, when it talks here about security or obligations of security, it has nothing to do, obligations of security, with respect to this noun "prisoners," and you're saying -- and is it your testimony that the security they're talking about in this case is security to be provided for the restoration of the terrain, which is a separate and independent thought, I would suggest to you, from the discussion that is being highlighted here, which is that there's prisoners in the schools? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't at all, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your entire analysis hinges on if after the word "security" someone of would have placed a comma or the words "as well as," then you would think that those are two independent thoughts. But I suggest to you, sir, that, the words or phrase "as well as" appears prior to "security," which really indicates that it's the prisoners that the security concern is for, and then the use of the word "and" is a separate independent thought, so it's a compound sentence. Perhaps a period should have been right after the word "security," and then the next thought would have been "restoration of the terrain," which would then make this paragraph having more than one sentence in it. Wouldn't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: And you never allowed me to say why I don't agree. First of all, with regard to your previous question, whether "prisoners" is a noun, one should say that this is just one form of that particular noun. But in this particular case, it could be out of the context. It is a genitive singular or a genitive plural. It could be both, but let me tell you the meaning of the context here. There's a multiple meaning, and it points to the fact that in this case genitive is a plural. The second thing that I don't agree on and you're not allowing me to say why, I didn't say that security is tied to the restoration. But rather, that both security and restoration are tied to the form terrain. And one additional evidence that this analysis is completely accurate is your completely objective translator who has translated the text who has translated the sentence absolutely correctly. Security and restoration of the terrain is a whole in which case security is one attribute of the terrain as well as restoration. So this is the structure comprising both security and restoration of the terrain. I don't know how else I could translate or utter this. I'm absolutely sure that from the expert of monolinguistic analysis or the feeling for the Serbian language, it is absolutely correct and true. Of course, one can translate from the Serbian into English correctly or subjectively or incorrectly. I did not analyse the translation, mind you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the first phrase in that paragraph number 6, I believe, which says "an additional burden," and it goes on, obviously. We got a proofing note yesterday after your meeting with counsel for Mr. Pandurevic, and it states as follows: "He ..." meaning you, Mr. Marojevic, "... looked at and further explained section 6 of the report. He said that the 'additional burden' in paragraph 6 was not at the same level as the responsibilities described in the first five paragraphs, as it was a worry rather than a responsibility. It was a secondary rather than a primary consideration." Is that what you told them yesterday or whenever?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I said that and that is indeed the case, and you can conclude that from at least two things, and one would suffice. The only -- this passage contains the word "additionally." "Additionally" is -- is part of a different style, something that would be appropriate for a footnote. This could have been under the text as a footnote. And the second word is "burden." One meaning of burden comes from physics. However, this burden is concern more than anything else. "Additional burden" generates concern about what might happen. So this is an additional concern. What concern is that a large number of prisoners deployed or billeted in schools --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, if you objectively look at the prior paragraph, they are discussing in the prior -- five paragraphs, but in the fifth paragraph they're discussing an attack by the enemy, and in fact he writes in this report that they repelled or repulsed that attack successfully, so what was the worry with the attack of the Bosnian Muslims? If you've defeated them militarily, wouldn't the worry be more primarily to be with respect to the POWs that were in the schools? Isn't that the only burden that was left for them at that time? Because if you look at paragraph 5, in the middle of it, it talks about repelling. It's in your report, but in the P329 it uses the word "repulsed successfully so far."

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if we followed your route and analysed from the end to the beginning of the document, I hope that we will come to the relationship between the 8th and the 7th. Now we are analysing the relationship between the 6th, 5th, and the 4th paragraphs. Please pay attention. All the brigade forces are fully engaged. This is five, and you have confused the passages. All the brigade forces are completely or fully engaged. What does it mean, fully engaged? It means that it's not just one unit that is engaged, but fully engaged. And we have no reserves, you know, that reserves are not on the front-line. They should be a bit further from the front-line. This means that the back is not protected. There are no reserves, and all the forces are fully engaged. This is your fifth paragraph that you have confused with passage 4. And in the fourth paragraph again, there is this additional burden, and it's very clear from the linguistic point of view. Look at the fourth -- actually, the fifth -- no, the fourth. With all available forces -- you know the meaning of "all," so with all available forces we have sealed off. If the enemy forces had not been strong, they would not have used all available forces, and they say that they sealed off the wider area of Crni Vrh and Planinica and partially the area of Kamenica. The weight of the previous paragraphs is completely understandable and is not matched by the subsequent passage, which just increases the argument when he asks for additional equipment and personnel because he doesn't have anybody in reserve. Have you ever served an army? Do you know what reserves means? Do you know what logistics means, what the meaning of the reserve is? Can I ask you? I believe that this is clear. It does not warn any further explanation, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I did say paragraph 5, but really, when I talked about repelling the enemy combatants, it appears in paragraph 3, you're right to say that there was a block or, as they put it on P329, they sealed off the wider area. My point is, sir, once they repelled the enemy combatants, once they completely and totally, as you say, blocked the area, really, the only concern left was the concern of the prisoners in the schools; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Again, you are not right because you are taking one part of the paragraph out of its context. In future, could you please read the whole paragraph? You said that a paragraph is one whole. Nobody contested that. That's why I'm asking you to read the whole paragraph, which would show you that so far the attacks had been repelled. But what will happen in the future, nobody knows. Please read from the beginning, in the text were regularly supported by all calibres of artillery and tanks, which means all calibres and tanks. I hope that you understand, that you appreciate what I'm saying, that acts of varying intensity followed one other, which means varying intensity. I suppose that I as a linguist should know that and you as a lawyer, of course, you're my opponent here, but you should know that. And then it says the attack on [indiscernible] is still in progress. Do you know the meaning of the term "in progress"? They have been repelled, but they have not been neutralised because they are still in progress. If you take something out of the context, one sentence or something else, and the paragraph is a whole, you cannot look at anything without a whole, then what you're doing is you're trying to misinterpret or you are trying to make me misinterpret a text. Please take a paragraph as a whole, and then you will be given an answer. The paragraph in itself will give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your answers are becoming longer and longer and longer, and you are engaging in arguments with the Defence counsel, who has got a right to put any question to you that is allowed by the Court. So you either conclude here, Mr. Ostojic, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: A few more questions. Just a few more, Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I know, sir, I'm not going to read out the entire paragraph. We're familiar with it. I just wanted to point out certain things for you. If you look, the interim combat report of the 15th July, 1995, was that written, sir, in the past, present, or future tense?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: I could take things in turn one by one, but I don't think that the Trial Chamber has the time for it. I would be able to tell you which verbs are in present, which in past, and which in future tense.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you look at the paragraph that you spent sometime analysing, paragraph 6, and it's just that one sentence. I know it's a little long and maybe compound, but that one sentence, you think that was written in past, present, or future tense when it references prisoners distributed throughout the schools. And actually, it says: An additional burden for us is the large number of prisoners distributed throughout schools in the brigade area." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: It says "they represent." The future tense would be "will represent." This is a present, but it is not a temporarily well defined. It is, rather, something that started in the past, continues, and will probably continue being a fact. So this is an extratemporal present tense.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So at the time of the writing of this report, the prisoners are alive and distributed throughout the schools. That's the plain and obvious read of this, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: In any case, one could read it a bit differently. The person writing this report speaks about them as living. There's no background information. He doesn't have any contact with the fact. He starts from the fact that the prisoners are there, that they are distributed in various schools, and that they represent or that they constituted a bad end for the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The past tense usage of that sentence in essence would have been that an additional burden was the prisoners who were at the school, et cetera, right? You would just use that word instead of the present-tense use of the word "is." You told us about the future, so now we're just talking about the past, right? Or you could have said it by using the word "were": An additional burden for us were the prisoners at the school. Then would know he's talking about a past tense, an event that happened before; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that would be the past tense, but here we have a present. The sentence is "the additional burden are..." but the word "now" is missing. If there was word "now," then the present would be narrowed down. This verb "are" does not pin-point the present time, but in any case it does comprise present as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Two or three more questions, I think, and I'm done. If we could just quickly look at P330, and thank you, Mr. President. P330, which is the 16th of July, 1995, report that you looked at when you did this intratextual analysis as one of your methods of your report. And I think when you looked at this, you were trying to compare it, and you -- and obviously, and especially from your report, it certainly seems you spent sometime reading it and digesting it, but if you look on and if you look -- doing a contextual analysis of this report, you look that the author mentions 7.000 combatants, civilians, and soldiers in the first paragraph; that's identified with the number 1, and then if you look at the third paragraph, they talk about - and I know you spent a significant amount of time - of letting go or releasing of 5.000 enemy combatants. Do you, sir, from reading this get the idea of what happened to the difference between the 7 and the 5, the 7.000 that were present and the 5.000 that were let go? Where are the 2.000 remaining soldiers and civilians?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please jog my memory. Where do they refer to the 5.000?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure if you are looking at the correct one. I'm looking at the 16th July report.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In the first paragraph numbered 1, it talks about: "Using their numerical advantage, they surrounded the 4th Battalion counting soldiers and civilians armed and unarmed altogether about 7.000." And then in the third paragraph, when they are discussing opening the corridor, it says "opening the corridor along the line of the three lost trenches for the civilian population, about 5.000 of them." And just I wanted to get -- draw from you based on your methodology of work contextually and even intratexturally, you know they mentioned on the 15th of July 3.000 people who were coming from behind. Now they're talking about 7.000 and 5.000. What happened to the -- contextually speaking, to the 2.000 remaining soldiers and civilians?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Before I answer your question, I have to say that you did not take these figures out of the context. We have to see what they refer to. An elementary analysis shows that under item 1, when it says using the numerical advantage they surrounded soldiers and civilians, armed and unarmed, altogether about 7.000. So they're talking about soldiers and civilians, 7.000 of them altogether. And then in order to justify his case before his command, having let them go through, he says that three trenches had been lost, that the corridor was open to the civilian population, and there were about 5.000 civilians. He points to the fact that there were about 5.000 civilians, and this is his justification for letting them through. This mean that is there were 2.000 soldiers. But it doesn't say here that he never let the soldiers go through. He doesn't specify the soldiers. He says that he let the civilians go through, and the soldiers went with them unless some of them were killed. The context is very clear. If that had been the subject of my analysis, if I had had this document, I would have paid attention to that, I would have established my facts, and then you would never have to ask me the question. The difference in the figures is completely clear. The first figure speaks about soldiers as the most important ones; then about civilians, some of them armed, the others unarmed; and then the second figure speaks about the opening of the corridor for the civilian population and the fact that some soldiers also passed through is not his fault, and there are 5.000 civilians. He did not say that there were 5.000 civilians and soldiers to contradict himself. He said there were 5.000 civilians. He may have arrived at the information subsequently. He could not have known how many --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we had a clear answer straightaway in the beginning, and he has repeated it three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honour. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Will you finish today, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I hope so, Mr. President. I'm going to discussion that with my co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Will you please try to make a humongous effort and finish today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'll make that effort, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you, Your Honours. Good afternoon to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you, Professor Marojevic. I only have a few questions. First, let me introduce myself is as is the custom. My name is Kweku Vanderpuye. On behalf of the Prosecution, I'll put some questions to you in respect of your report, in respect of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If there's anything that I ask you that's unclear to you, let me know, and I'll try to rephrase it in a way that you can better understand it. Prior to testifying here today, sir, did you follow the testimony of General Pandurevic in this trial?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: No, not at all. I rarely watch television except for sports programs, but I certainly don't watch trials.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In the preparation of your report, it's fair to say that you did not consider the testimony of General Krstic regarding his views -- regarding his views of the 15 July interim report that was the subject of your report?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: I not only did not take it into account, but I'm not familiar with his views. I analysed only these two reports, and I knew only them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You didn't take into consideration the testimony of General Radovan Radinovic in respect of his views concerning the same report; that's true, right?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO MAROJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct, and I don't know of his views.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution opposes the testimony of Mr. Marojevic as an expert in this case. We have full faith that the Court will accord the appropriate weight to the testimony as has been entered in the record in this case. We have no further cross-examination, as we don't feel that it will be fruitful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there re-examination, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you don't wish to comment on Mr. Vanderpuye's statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I understand his position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Do you have questions, Judge Kwon? Professor, we don't have any further questions for you, which basically means that your testimony ends here. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having come over to give testimony, and I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I -- in thinking about the motion of -- that Mr. Gosnell referred to and the document associated with the MUP, the dog document, as we call it, I realise that when -- it's 4104. When Mr. Momir Nikolic testifies, he will testify at length about the units, the forces at Potocari, along the road, and it would be our intention to use that document in our questioning of him. Therefore, I think it would be best to save any ruling on that document until after the testimony of Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Do you wish to comment, Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Well, first of all, we don't concede necessarily that the document would be admissible through any future witness, and it's premature, of course, to comment on that. But given what the Prosecution has just said, I think what they are saying is that they are content with the document being in e-court, being marked for identification, and not being an exhibit. In that case, I would be content for that to be the situation. But in a sense, I think that what that means is that you should sustain our objection and that the document should not be considered admitted and that it does remain, of course, in e-court as with any other document that's uploaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maybe we are all tired, but I didn't think --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I must be tired because that sounded like a bunch of legal gobbledy-gook to me. We don't need to enter it into evidence. It just stays where it is. We'll deal with it at the end of that other testimony, and we can argue about it then. Why argue about it now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Having heard what you had to say, the document will remain MFI'd, and we'll decide in due course if it becomes necessary. Documents, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. In relation to the last witness, I don't know if an e-mail has yet gone out, but there are only two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't seen any e-mails.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's 7D778, the curriculum vitae of Professor Marojevic, and 7D917, the report with attachments. The only reason we called him at all was in response to Judge Prost's question. The report and attachment was translated by the translation service of this Tribunal. I would invite her attention to attachment number 1, paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Any objections from any of the other Defence teams?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm very sorry. I apparently used another document, 7D775, the mobilisation order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You did, in fact. Any objection? Objections from Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have the same objection as I made with respect to the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But he has given evidence in any case now, so I think the documents have to -- yes, exactly. So the documents are admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have any documents that you wish to tender, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think we've seen the articles. I don't think it would be necessary. But thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm sorry, I hope we've completed the tendering process. There was one issue I wanted to bring to the attention of the Court and also to my colleagues. But I don't want to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We have been discussing with the Miletic team the possibly of reaching a stipulation with respect to convoy-related documents that we think are important for the Court to have in terms of assessing the convoy approval process, the players that are involved, et cetera. I just wanted to let you know that we are currently trying to sort that out. We expect that we will arrive at something relatively soon. But I just didn't want to take you by surprise when we are completed -- when we've completed the process. We're also talking to the Gvero team with respect to those documents as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Incidentally, Mr. McCloskey, before we proceed with the next thing we have in mind, is yesterday Ms. Nikolic made some submissions in relation to 3D556 after having withdrawn her request in relation to 3D555. You were supposed to think about it and come back to us in a final way. Have you done -- are you in a position to give us your final position?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we've just reached an agreement. We don't have any objection to the material she would like from -- the short material from the testimony of General Hadzihasanovic. No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So having heard that, we are going to dispose now of the various other issues relating to various documents. We start with documents 2D639, 2D644, 2D645, all being documents tendered by the Beara Defence team to which the Prosecution objected. After deliberations, we have come to the conclusion not to admit any of these three documents on the following grounds: 2D639, this is, as you will recall, the interview of Milos Tomovic. The Beara Defense team, Mr. Ostojic actually read a limited part of this interview into the record, as you recall. The Trial Chamber then disallowed further use of the interview upon objection by the Prosecution and the Pandurevic Defence team. To the extent that limited use of the document was permitted, that portion of the interview was read directly into the record, and we see no need for having the interview admitted into the record, and that is the reason for dismissing the Beara Defence team's request. Second document is 2D644, which is a statement on information of Bruce Bursik regarding an interview with the person I mentioned before, Milos Tomovic; and 2D645, which is another statement of Milos Tomovic. Having gone through this transcript, we come the conclusion that neither of these two documents were put to the witness, and circumstances being what they are, we do not see a reason why they should be admitted into the records as exhibits. The Nikolic issue has now been agreed upon, so we don't need to decide upon it. And 3D556 is therefore being admitted into the records. We have a last document, which is a Prosecution document, P4402, to which the Gvero Defence team objected and submitted that if admitted, the documents used should be limited to matters of the credibility of the witness. As you will recall, P4402 is an extract from Karadzic's handwritten notes of a meeting held in 1992 which show that Pandurevic was present. The document was shown to witness Pandurevic who did not deny that he was present at the meeting. Although the notes also appear to suggest the presence of General Gvero at the meeting, the Trial Chamber finds that admitting the document without any restrictions is not unfairly prejudicial to Gvero, especially considering what General Pandurevic himself testified on this issue. So that disposes of the pending issues relating to documents, leaving the one raised by Mr. Gosnell in deep freeze for the time being as we explained earlier on. Now, tomorrow, as we had intimated to you, we are not sitting. I take it, Mr. Haynes, you don't have any further witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, but I would like to trouble you for a minute or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Shall I do that now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: My focus has been elsewhere for the last ten days, and the Prosecution's motion for rebuttal and re-opening actually impacts upon my client's case probably rather more than anybody else's, and I've seen and heard your remarks from yesterday. I will do my very best in the next 24 hours to file something, but I'm not making any promises that it will come before the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Mr. Haynes. That's fair enough. I measured my words yesterday. I did not tell that you needed to, only that it would be preferable if you did. But of course, we did not shorten the time-limit, and the time-limit therefore remains. However, any filings before that date will be helpful. All right. And I take it, because you haven't answered my question, you don't have further --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. I need to attend to some technical difficulties with some 92 bis statements, but other than that and subject to any remarkable departure in my instructions, that's all the evidence I'm going to present other than, as I say, some 92 bis statements and a bar table motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. There is no way we can hear your remaining witness on the re-opening any time soon? I think you indicated that you would want that in the week starting on the 23rd, Mr. McCloskey; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can go into private session on that briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for awhile. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So for the time being, there are no sittings scheduled for next week, as I see it, unless there are matters, urgent matters that arise that need to be addressed. We will be working on the rebuttal motion, of course, and we hope to be in a position to come down with our decision as early as possible. But we necessarily and you have necessarily got to earmark the following week for any further business to transact depending, of course, on our decision on rebuttal. We stand adjourned. Thank you.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.19 p.m.
